articles.title: Indian solar mission's new findings throw light on enduring Sun mysteries
articles.summary: Why is the Sun's corona millions of degrees hotter than its surface? And how does it maintain its inexplicably high temperature?
articles.content:
One of the most enduring mysteries that has been puzzling scientists forever is how the Sun's outer atmosphere - the corona - is millions of degrees hotter than its surface. And how does the corona continue to remain so hot despite frequent eruptions during which it loses huge amounts of energy?

Astrophysicists in India now say the latest findings from Aditya-L1, the country's first solar observation mission in space, have provided them some vital clues to unlocking those mysteries. Their findings are revealed in a recent paper published in the prestigious Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The temperature variations in different regions of the Sun defy the laws of physics, says leading Indian solar astrophysicist Prof R Ramesh of the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) who led the study.

If you cut through the Sun's layers, deep inside is the core where the temperature is 15 million Celsius. Travel outwards to the surface or the photosphere - the part that we see from the Earth - it's about 5,500C. Far away from the core is the Sun's outermost layer or corona where the temperature is about 2 million C - it can sometimes go up to 40 million C.

Prof Ramesh says the corona is where extreme weather events - such as solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) - originate, during which large amounts of energy is released by the Sun into space. The CMEs cause beautiful auroras, and they can also affect life on Earth by causing geomagnetic storms that can knock down power grids and affect weather and communication satellites.

In normal or low-activity times, the Sun launches two to three CMEs a day. During the maximum solar activity cycle that comes every 11 years, there can be 10 or more in a single day.

"Now if the Sun is losing such huge amounts of energy with each CME and it's not replenished, the star at the centre of our solar system would lose all its energy and Earth would plunge into an irreversible deep freeze," Prof Ramesh says.

But since that's not happening, it means there's a "mechanism" by which the corona is able to maintain its inexplicably high temperature, he says.

articles.personality_title: India's Aditya-L1 mission reveals new clues about the Sun's hottest layer
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long wondered why the Sun's outer atmosphere, called the corona, is millions of degrees hotter than its surface. This is puzzling because the corona loses a lot of energy through eruptions but still stays extremely hot.

**What happened** – India's first space mission dedicated to studying the Sun, called Aditya-L1, recently sent back important new information. A team led by Professor R Ramesh from the Indian Institute of Astrophysics studied this data and published their findings in a top science journal.

**Impact** – The mission helped show that the Sun has a special way of keeping its corona very hot, even though it loses energy during solar eruptions called coronal mass ejections (CMEs). These eruptions can affect Earth by causing auroras and sometimes disrupting power and satellite systems. Understanding how the corona stays hot helps scientists better predict these space weather events.

**What's next step** – Researchers will continue studying data from Aditya-L1 to learn more about the Sun’s behavior. This could improve forecasts of solar storms that impact Earth and help protect technology that people rely on.

**One-sentence takeaway** – India's Aditya-L1 mission has provided key insights into how the Sun's corona remains extremely hot despite powerful energy losses during solar eruptions.
articles.personality_title_fr: La mission Aditya-L1 de l'Inde révèle de nouveaux indices sur la couche la plus chaude du Soleil
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques se demandent depuis longtemps pourquoi l'atmosphère extérieure du Soleil, appelée la couronne, est des millions de degrés plus chaude que sa surface. C'est surprenant car la couronne perd beaucoup d'énergie lors d'éruptions mais reste très chaude.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – La première mission spatiale indienne dédiée à l'étude du Soleil, nommée Aditya-L1, a récemment envoyé des informations importantes. Une équipe dirigée par le professeur R Ramesh de l'Institut indien d'astrophysique a étudié ces données et publié leurs résultats dans une revue scientifique renommée.

**Impact** – La mission a montré que le Soleil possède un mécanisme spécial pour garder sa couronne très chaude, même s'il perd de l'énergie lors d'éruptions solaires appelées éjections de masse coronale (EMC). Ces éruptions peuvent affecter la Terre en provoquant des aurores et parfois en perturbant les réseaux électriques et les satellites. Comprendre comment la couronne reste chaude aide les scientifiques à mieux prévoir ces phénomènes.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs continueront d'étudier les données d'Aditya-L1 pour mieux comprendre le comportement du Soleil. Cela pourrait améliorer les prévisions des tempêtes solaires qui touchent la Terre et aider à protéger les technologies utilisées par les gens.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La mission Aditya-L1 de l'Inde a apporté des indices clés sur la façon dont la couronne du Soleil reste extrêmement chaude malgré les fortes pertes d'énergie lors des éruptions solaires.
articles.personality_title_es: La misión Aditya-L1 de India revela nuevas pistas sobre la capa más caliente del Sol
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han preguntado durante mucho tiempo por qué la atmósfera exterior del Sol, llamada corona, está a millones de grados más caliente que su superficie. Esto es extraño porque la corona pierde mucha energía durante erupciones pero aún así se mantiene muy caliente.

**Qué pasó** – La primera misión espacial de India dedicada a estudiar el Sol, llamada Aditya-L1, envió recientemente información importante. Un equipo liderado por el profesor R Ramesh del Instituto Indio de Astrofísica estudió estos datos y publicó sus hallazgos en una revista científica reconocida.

**Impacto** – La misión mostró que el Sol tiene un mecanismo especial para mantener su corona muy caliente, a pesar de perder energía durante erupciones solares llamadas eyecciones de masa coronal (CME). Estas erupciones pueden afectar la Tierra causando auroras y a veces interrumpiendo redes eléctricas y satélites. Entender cómo la corona se mantiene caliente ayuda a los científicos a predecir mejor estos eventos.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán estudiando los datos de Aditya-L1 para aprender más sobre el comportamiento del Sol. Esto podría mejorar las predicciones de tormentas solares que afectan la Tierra y ayudar a proteger la tecnología que usamos.

**Resumen en una frase** – La misión Aditya-L1 de India ha dado pistas importantes sobre cómo la corona del Sol se mantiene extremadamente caliente a pesar de perder mucha energía durante las erupciones solares.
